question: How many hearts does an octopus have?
source_excerpt: The octopuses' largest heart, the systemic heart, is located in the middle of the mollusk's body. It pumps oxygenated blood around the body, but not to the gills.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume every animal runs on a single pump; the octopus turns out to be running a small plumbing network.
extra.verification_notes: Octopuses have three hearts (one systemic, two branchial), confirmed by https://www.livescience.com/how-many-hearts-does-an-octopus-have

explanation: Two of them push blood through the gills, and the third sends it around the rest of the body.

question: Which gas makes up roughly four fifths of the air you are breathing right now?
source_excerpt: The composition of Earth's atmosphere by volume is 78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen, 0.93% argon, 0.04% carbon dioxide

extra.why_interesting: The instinctive guess is oxygen, the gas we care about, but most of every breath is something we simply exhale again unused.
extra.verification_notes: Nitrogen is ~78% of air by volume, consistent with the standard reference (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmosphere_of_Earth); 'roughly four fifths' is a fair approximation.

explanation: Oxygen is only about a fifth of the air, so most of every breath goes in and straight back out untouched.

question: Which appeared on Earth first: the first sharks, or the first trees?
source_excerpt: the earliest fossil evidence for sharks or their ancestors is a few scales dating to 450 million years ago, during the Late Ordovician Period.

extra.why_interesting: Trees feel like ancient scenery and sharks like animals; in fact sharks were patrolling the oceans tens of millions of years before the first forest grew.
extra.verification_notes: Sharks (scales ~450 Mya, undisputed ~420 Mya) predate the earliest trees (~385 Mya, Devonian), so the answer holds.

explanation: Sharks go back roughly 450 million years, while the first true trees only appeared around 385 million years ago, so sharks had the seas to themselves long before any forest existed.

question: Thanks to its overseas territories, which country spans more time zones than any other, beating even Russia and the United States?
source_excerpt: Owing to the number of territories it governs beyond Europe, France has 12 (and for a period of the year 13) time zones.

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Russia or the USA, but the overseas territories scattered across the Pacific, Indian Ocean and Caribbean hand the title to a mid-sized European country.
extra.verification_notes: Guinness World Records confirms France has the most time zones (12, or 13 with daylight saving), ahead of Russia and the US with 11 each; https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/584626-country-with-the-most-time-zones

explanation: Counting territories from French Polynesia to New Caledonia and French Guiana, France covers twelve time zones, one more than Russia.

question: Which country has the longest coastline in the world, long enough to wrap around the equator about five times?
source_excerpt: 243,042 kilometers, or 151,019 miles of coastline

extra.why_interesting: Players picture island nations like Indonesia or the sheer width of Russia, but Canada's Arctic archipelago and fjord-cut shores stretch far enough to circle the Earth five times.
extra.verification_notes: Canada has the longest coastline under every measure; the 'about five times' multiplier matches the CIA Factbook figure of 202,080 km, though Statistics Canada's 243,042 km gives about six, so the clause is slightly source-dependent.

explanation: Its thousands of Arctic islands and deeply indented shores add up to roughly 200,000 kilometres, more than double Indonesia in second place.

question: Archaeologists opening ancient Egyptian tombs have found pots of which everyday food still perfectly edible after about 3,000 years?
source_excerpt: Honey from sealed Egyptian tombs is still edible after 3,000 years

extra.why_interesting: Everything in a tomb seems like it should have crumbled to dust, yet one everyday kitchen staple came out perfectly preserved.
extra.verification_notes: Honey is the standard answer and the only plausible candidate, and its preservation chemistry is well established, though the specific 'tasted and edible' tomb discovery is folklore and not documented (see boingboing/scienceblog sources).

explanation: Honey is so low in water and so acidic that bacteria and mould simply cannot grow in it, which is why a sealed jar effectively never spoils.

question: True or false: an Olympic gold medal is made mostly of gold.
source_excerpt: gold medals must be made with at least 92.5 percent silver and contain at least six grams of gold

extra.why_interesting: The name says gold, the colour says gold, but the prize is a silver medal wearing a thin golden coat.

topicality.rationale: General sports trivia, not tied to recent news.

extra.verification_notes: IOC rules require gold medals to be at least 92.5% silver with a minimum of 6 g gold plating, so they are not mostly gold (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_medal).

explanation: The rules require a gold medal to be at least 92.5 percent silver, coated with only about six grams of actual gold.

question: At the 1968 Olympics, American Dick Fosbury shocked the crowd by going over the bar backwards and won gold in which athletics event?
source_excerpt: Dick Fosbury won the gold medal in the men's high jump at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics, setting an Olympic record of 2.24 m.

extra.why_interesting: The stem gives the footholds, backwards over a bar, and the player realises that the odd-looking technique they have seen on TV once got an athlete laughed at.
extra.verification_notes: Fosbury, an American, won the 1968 Olympic men's high jump gold using the backward 'Fosbury flop' technique (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Fosbury).

explanation: People laughed at his back-first style, but the Fosbury Flop was so effective that almost every elite jumper has used it ever since.

question: In which year did Mickey Mouse make his famous debut whistling at the wheel of a boat in the cartoon Steamboat Willie?
source_excerpt: Steamboat Willie premiered on November 18, 1928, at the Colony Theater in New York City.

extra.why_interesting: Mickey feels like a product of the colour-TV era, but he whistled his way onto screens before the Great Depression had even started.
extra.verification_notes: Steamboat Willie premiered November 18, 1928, which Disney treats as Mickey's official debut (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steamboat_Willie).

explanation: Steamboat Willie premiered in New York in November 1928, one of the very first cartoons with fully synchronised sound.

question: In The Simpsons, which musical instrument is Lisa Simpson famous for playing?
source_excerpt: Her hobbies include reading and playing the baritone saxophone.

extra.why_interesting: A simple pop-culture check; the player hears a riff from the opening titles in their head and the answer drops out.
extra.verification_notes: Lisa Simpson is famously a saxophonist (baritone sax per Wikipedia), and nothing newer contradicts this.

explanation: Lisa's instrument is specifically a baritone saxophone, and her solo in the opening titles is one of the show's longest-running gags.

question: The shortest war in recorded history was fought between Britain and Zanzibar in 1896. Roughly how long did it last?
source_excerpt: The war lasted roughly 38 to 45 minutes on 27 August 1896, considered the shortest war in recorded history.

extra.why_interesting: The word war implies months or years; a player who guesses days feels bold, and the truth, shorter than a football match, beats them.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia gives the Anglo-Zanzibar War as 38–45 minutes on 27 Aug 1896, and it is regarded as the shortest recorded war, so 'Under an hour' is correct.

explanation: British warships began bombarding the sultan's palace in the morning and the fighting was over in about 40 minutes, shorter than a football match.

question: The ostrich lays the biggest egg of any bird, but which flightless bird lays the largest egg compared with its own body size, around a fifth of its weight?
source_excerpt: one of the largest eggs in proportion to its size of any bird in the world

extra.why_interesting: The ostrich wins on absolute size, which is the player's reflex, but proportionally the champion is a chicken-sized flightless bird on the other side of the world.
extra.verification_notes: Kiwi is the flightless bird with the proportionally largest egg (up to ~20% of female weight); petrels that may exceed it can fly, so the 'flightless' qualifier holds (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiwi_(bird)).

explanation: A kiwi egg can take up so much of the female's body that she cannot eat properly in the final days before laying it.

question: Which country produces more olive oil than any other, usually close to half of the entire world's supply?
source_excerpt: world olive oil production in the 2025/26 crop year is expected to be around 3,440,000 tonnes

extra.why_interesting: Marketing and restaurant menus make Italy the obvious guess, but the country that actually fills most of the world's bottles is next door.
extra.verification_notes: Spain remains the largest olive oil producer (about 40% of world output in 2025/26 per FAO/IOC data), so 'close to half' is loose but acceptable.

explanation: Italy gets the glamour, but Spain, especially the region of Andalusia, out-produces every other country by a wide margin.

question: Which river passes through more countries than any other in the world, ten in total, on its way to the Black Sea?
source_excerpt: Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova, and Ukraine

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for giants like the Nile or Amazon, but the record for crossing borders belongs to a European river many of them have stood beside.
extra.verification_notes: The Danube is widely documented as flowing through ten countries, the most of any river; no contradicting or newer information found (https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Danube_River).

explanation: From Germany's Black Forest to the Black Sea it also passes four capital cities: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.

question: Which South Korean film about a poor family scheming its way into a rich household became the first non-English-language movie ever to win the Oscar for Best Picture?
source_excerpt: Parasite becomes first non-English language film to win best picture Oscar

extra.why_interesting: After more than ninety ceremonies dominated by English, the barrier finally fell to a South Korean thriller about a family of con artists.

topicality.rationale: 2020 Oscar win, no fresher today than a year ago.

extra.verification_notes: Parasite won Best Picture at the 92nd Oscars (2020) as the first non-English-language winner; no later event can change this historical first.

explanation: Bong Joon-ho's film took four Oscars in 2020, including Best Picture, something no film in a language other than English had managed in over ninety years.

question: When Pope Gregory introduced his new calendar in 1582, people went to bed on the fourth of October and woke up on the fifteenth. How many days were skipped?
source_excerpt: Thursday 4 October 1582 was followed by Friday 15 October 1582 (10 days skipped)

extra.why_interesting: The idea that ten dates simply never happened is hard to believe, yet it is why a few countries celebrate certain holidays on different days to this day.
extra.verification_notes: Gregorian reform skipped 5–14 October 1582, i.e. 10 days, per Wikipedia's Gregorian calendar article.

explanation: The old Julian calendar had drifted about ten days from the solar year, so those dates were simply deleted to put Easter back in line with the spring equinox.

question: Not counting the Sun, what is the brightest star in the night sky, found in the constellation of the Great Dog?
source_excerpt: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky, located in the southern constellation of Canis Major.

extra.why_interesting: The reflex guess is the North Star, which is actually fairly dim; the real champion is the dog star low in the winter sky.
extra.verification_notes: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky and is in Canis Major (the Great Dog), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirius.

explanation: Sirius outshines the famous North Star many times over, mostly because it is one of our nearest stellar neighbours at under nine light-years away.

question: Which country became the first in the world to give all adult women the right to vote in national elections, back in 1893?
source_excerpt: New Zealand became the first nation in the world to grant women the right to vote in national elections when the Governor, Lord Glasgow, gave Royal Assent to an Electoral Bill on 19 September 1893.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect a European revolutionary nation or the United States, but the breakthrough came from a small colony at the far end of the Pacific, decades before Britain or America.
extra.verification_notes: New Zealand was the first self-governing nation to grant women the vote in national elections (Electoral Act, 19 Sept 1893); no later event changes this (https://gg.govt.nz/node/409).

explanation: New Zealand women were voting a quarter of a century before Britain and the United States followed, and the campaign's leader, Kate Sheppard, now appears on the country's ten-dollar note.

question: Since a 2022 agreement over a tiny Arctic island, Canada has a land border with a second country besides the United States. Which country?
source_excerpt: Canada and the Kingdom of Denmark, together with Greenland, reach historic agreement on long-standing boundary disputes

extra.why_interesting: Everyone 'knows' Canada has exactly one land neighbour, the United States. The answer flips that, and a player who remembers where Greenland sits can reason their way to it.

topicality.rationale: Hans Island border deal is a 2022 geography fact, no fresher today than a year ago.

extra.verification_notes: The 2022 Hans Island agreement gave Canada its first land border with Denmark (via Greenland, part of the Kingdom of Denmark); no newer event found that overturns this.

explanation: Canada and Denmark ended their long, mostly friendly fight over Hans Island between Ellesmere Island and Greenland by simply drawing a line across it, so the two countries now meet on land.

question: Venus comes nearer to Earth than any other planet at its closest approach. But averaged over many years, which planet spends the most time closest to Earth?
source_excerpt: Venus is on average 1.14 AU from Earth, but Mercury is a much closer 1.04 AU.

extra.why_interesting: Almost everyone answers Venus because it makes the closest approach. The stem's word 'averaged' is the foothold: a player who pictures the orbits realises the innermost planet can never wander far away.

topicality.rationale: Orbital-mechanics science fact with no news hook.

extra.verification_notes: Physics Today (2019) shows Mercury is on average the nearest planet to Earth (~1.04 AU vs Venus ~1.14 AU), while Venus has the closest single approach, consistent with the question.

explanation: Mercury hugs the Sun so tightly that it is never farther from Earth than the Sun is, while Venus and Mars spend long periods on the opposite side of the Sun, pushing their average distance up.
